abstract: Species delineation and taxonomy are notoriously complicated, especially for fossils where available information is often limited to morphology. However, palaeogenomics can add a genetic dimension to fossils, which allows for both robust resolution of taxonomy and trait functional characterization. In this study, we present the two first ancient genomes from voucher specimens morphologically attributed to the extinct yak Bos mutus baikalensis. We demonstrate that this taxon falls within the genetic variation of yak X, a cryptic bovine species previously identified using genetics solely from non-diagnostic bone fragments. We collate morphological, palaeontological, geographical, and genomic data available from both Bos mutus baikalensis and yak X in order to fully describe this species, which we propose be named as the lowland yak (Bos baikalensis). We further characterize genomic regions that may have been under natural selection or underlie functional differences in the lowland yak compared to the extant wild mountain and domestic yaks (B. mutus and B. grunniens, respectively) and other bovines. We find signals of functional changes in genes related to hypoxia, appetite control, morphology, fat metabolism, temperature, olfaction, immunity, and reproduction.
